England.difference_en: England specifies multiplication tables progressively: 2, 5 and 10 in Year 2; 3, 4 and 8 in Year 3; up to 12×12 in Year 4.
England.why_en: Facts expand through related structures, commutativity and multiples rather than as a single undifferentiated list.
England.classroom_use_en: After recall practice, derive an unknown fact from a known one, such as using 6×4 to find 7×4.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 requires fluency with multiplication and division facts within 100.
US.why_en: The same grade also develops operation properties, so facts can be related and derived.
US.classroom_use_en: Link multiplication facts to inverse division facts and neighbouring facts.

England.difference_en: England develops division facts alongside the corresponding multiplication tables.
England.why_en: Inverse relationships mean division facts do not need to be treated as a completely separate memory set.
England.classroom_use_en: After each multiplication fact, write the two related division facts.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 develops multiplication and division facts together and explicitly connects the operations.
US.why_en: One fact family supports multiplication, division and unknown-factor reasoning.
US.classroom_use_en: Give 24 and generate related multiplication and division statements.

England.difference_en: England uses commutative, associative and distributive structures in facts and calculation, with guidance using representations to expose those relationships.
England.why_en: Operation properties allow pupils to transform an unfamiliar calculation into known facts.
England.classroom_use_en: Use an array to explain why 7×6 can be decomposed into 5×6+2×6.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 explicitly requires operation properties as strategies for multiplication and division.
US.why_en: Properties are used as reasons for calculation methods, not only as vocabulary to memorise.
US.classroom_use_en: After decomposition, ask which relationship was used and why the product is unchanged.

England.difference_en: England moves into formal multiplication recording across Years 3-4 and uses long multiplication in Year 5. Current PEP has confirmed restructuring of some multi-digit multiplication content, but exact volume placement remains pending.
England.why_en: Formal algorithms compress place value and partial products.
England.classroom_use_en: Match each region of an area model to the corresponding partial-product line in the written method.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 still uses place-value/property-based multi-digit multiplication strategies; Grade 5 requires the standard multiplication algorithm.
US.why_en: Partial products and area models can explain the place value in each algorithm line before the compact method is required.
US.classroom_use_en: Ask why the second partial-product line represents tens rather than ones.

England.difference_en: England uses short division in Year 5 and long division in Year 6.
England.why_en: Written division requires connections among grouping, place value, partial quotients and remainders.
England.classroom_use_en: Estimate the quotient first, then explain the place value of each quotient digit.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 4-5 develop multi-digit division using place value, properties and models; Grade 6 requires the standard multi-digit division algorithm.
US.why_en: Partial quotients and models can make the compact algorithm interpretable.
US.classroom_use_en: Compare a partial-quotient method with the standard algorithm and identify the same multiples of the divisor.

England.difference_en: England progressively requires pupils to interpret remainders according to context, including whether a whole extra unit is needed.
England.why_en: A remainder is not just a final extra number; its meaning depends on the unit and question.
England.classroom_use_en: Use 22÷5 in two contexts: minimum vehicles needed and number of completely filled vehicles.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 includes whole-number division with remainders and problem interpretation.
US.why_en: The same quotient and remainder can lead to different real-world answers.
US.classroom_use_en: Require one sentence explaining what the remainder represents in every remainder problem.

England.difference_en: England uses multiplication and division in equal-group, scaling, combination and measurement problems and expects appropriate operation choice.
England.why_en: Recognising the multiplicative relationship is more reliable than looking for keywords.
England.classroom_use_en: Represent number of groups × amount per group = total before calculating.

US.difference_en: Common Core systematically develops multiplication/division problems from Grade 3 and extends them into multi-step, measurement, fraction and ratio contexts.
US.why_en: The number domain changes while the underlying multiplicative structure can remain the same.
US.classroom_use_en: Rewrite an integer multiplication problem in a measurement or fraction context and compare the structure.
